extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / Royal Society members, 17th-century scientists and mariners
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of observational reports, practical folk-knowledge, and navigational advice published in the Philosophical Transactions (1675); intended to report natural-history findings, agricultural and medicinal practices, and practical guidance for Arctic navigation to learned readers and mariners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Northeast passage route recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: The strait between Spitzberg and Nova-zembla (around 78°–80° N) may be passed and the course to be directed to the 78th, 79th, or 80th degrees of north latitude; drawing a line from our seas through the 78th or 79th degree of latitude to the Strait of Jezzo is near a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steering directly through the strait between Spitzberg and Nova-zembla gives a shorter course; alternatively, coasting along Tartary to find a strait may be longer but perhaps safer and better. This recommendation is based on reports and previous expeditions' experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for Arctic voyage
rubrics_metrics.description: The voyage ought to begin in the beginning of spring (viz. March) when winds and seas are favourable for sailing to Spitzberg and nearby polar regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may reach Spitzberg and return in 12–13 days if weather permits; if proceeding to the Straits of Jezzo one must steer south later and expect northern gales (often not until August). For shortest dispatch it's safest to choose a time enabling quick arrival at Spitzberg and prompt return; depart sooner if winds permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coasts; favor open seas to reduce ice risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots ought to shun all near approach to coasts and islands encountered for fear of the ice, and always make choice of the most open seas which are least infested with ice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows sea-coasts (due to fresh rivers and melted snows) freeze more readily than open seas; therefore open waters are generally safer and less likely to be blocked by ice floes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wintering shelter construction in Arctic
rubrics_metrics.description: If ships are forced to winter in the far north, inhabitants should sink their houses under ground and heap much earth over them rather than erect huts of thin boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dutch error of building exposed, thin-board huts contributed to hardship; burrowing dwellings insulated by earth are far better for subsistence in extreme northern winters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated voyage duration once sea known
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nature of the northern sea and its several straits shall be more perfectly discovered, the whole voyage to Japan may be performed in five or six weeks at the most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a conditional estimate based on improved knowledge of straits and currents; current known difficulties (ice, coasts) make durations longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ink-making from iris root
rubrics_metrics.description: To make ink: take the root of iris palustris lutea, infuse it 24 hours in clear fountain-water (or boil it a little); then rub a rough white pebble continually in the water on a knife or any piece of clean steel — in less than an hour the water becomes very black and tolerably good ink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, local method observed among highlanders; time of infusion and mechanical rubbing on steel produce the darkening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Herbal salve (Lancashire Asphodel) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A salve made from a certain common forest herb (identified as Asphodelus Lancastriae) reduced with wax and butter heals wounds very suddenly; it staunches bleeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it heals 'too suddenly' it is not advised for deep wounds (dangerous), but it is effective for superficial scars; proceed with caution when applying to deep lesions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of seaweed as manure (crop-specific effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seaweed dramatically increases barley yields (lands manured with seaweed yield l6–18 fold in some places), but lands often manured with seaweed yield poor oats and small quantities, with thicker husks and increased mixture of darnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seaweed appears especially effective on sandy soils for barley without further manure; however repeated use harms oat quality and quantity. Observers should consider crop-specific outcomes when using seaweed manure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairy-ring fungus spawn observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where fairy-rings are brown and almost bare, digging to about 2 inches reveals the spawn of the fungus of a greyish-white colour; where the grass has regrown green and rank, spawn was not found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or absence of fungal spawn correlates with surface appearance of the ring; digging to shallow depth can reveal fungal spawn responsible for the ring phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bark structure and function (Malpighi's anatomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bark is made of several parts, principally 'ligneous fibres' (analogous to nerves), which are pipes pervious to clear liquor divided into many square partitions; horizontal ranks of bags or bubbles append to these pipes where ascending juice is discharged and fermented into aliment; bark also increases plant bulk by adding yearly a coat or ring of fibres that become wood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Malpighi's descriptive model of plant bark and its role in transporting and preparing nutritive juices and in annual growth rings; used to interpret plant physiology and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stem composition and role of air-pipes (spiral fibres)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stem or trunk consists of ligneous fibres, transverse ranks of bubbles, and air-pipes (spiral fibres) — the latter constituting open hollow pipes capable of contraction and dilatation and likened to lungs; roots are especially stored with them and take in air chiefly from the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malpighi argues air stored in these pipes, subject to compression and rarefaction, presses upon adjacent woody fibres and bubbles and aids movement of juice; this underpins his view of the importance of air and 'respiration' in plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaves as sites of further concoction and 'skin' analog
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves perform the part of skin in animals: they contain air-vessels, woody-fibres, and vessels of transpiration and are places where the nutritious juice is further concocted; there may be a regress of concocted juice from leaves into the stem implying circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malpighi supports this with observations on seminal plants (two leaves) and uses it to explain leaf importance in plant nutrition and internal circulation of juices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowers and seeds as reproductive organs (uterus analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A blossom or flower is likened to a uterus together with the egg or fetus of the plant; seeds are lodged in various cases or caskets performing the office of a uterus; fruits are apparatus formed for the sake of the seed (the foetus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an interpretive anatomical analogy explaining generative structures in plants and their role in reproduction and fruit formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation of equality of natural days and meridian proposal critique
rubrics_metrics.description: A Spanish professor proposed adopting a common first meridian and asserted all natural days are of equal length (no equation of time) based on pendulum-clock observations; Mr. Flamsteed refutes the equality of the days and the absence of the equation of time on account of the obliquity of the ecliptic and the earth's unequal motion in her elliptical orbit, and finds the professor's instruments and lunar observations erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Astronomers will compute longitude from meridians of their own observatories; claim of universal meridian adoption is impracticable. Use obliquity and orbital eccentricity to demonstrate equation of time and assess instrument accuracy critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication required to support priority of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An assertion that an Englishman first found and caused watches with a spring-applied balance to be made years ago, but without printed description or successful subsequent improvements, does not amount to a clear priority over later published claims (e.g. Huygens' communicated invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical success and publication are important for establishing priority; unpublished or unsuccessful constructions weaken claims of precedence.
